Introduction
0:00
in this lecture we look at projectile motion
0:04
a projectile is any object thrown into the air and left to move under gravity alone
0:11
we will ignore air resistance throughout
0:15
so the only force acting after launch is the weight of the object
0:21
by the end you should be able to resolve a launch velocity into its horizontal and vertical components
0:29
derive the range equation for a launch from level ground
0:35
find the time of flight from the vertical motion
0:41
and find the maximum height reached
Resolving the velocity
0:48
start with a ball launched at speed u at an angle theta above the horizontal
0:55
I assume you already know how to resolve a vector into perpendicular components
1:02
the horizontal component of the velocity is u cos theta
1:08
and the vertical component is u sin theta
1:14
horizontally there is no force so the horizontal velocity stays constant for the whole flight
1:22
vertically the ball decelerates at g on the way up and accelerates at g on the way down
The range equation
3:50
now let's derive how far the ball travels before it lands
3:56
the horizontal distance is the horizontal velocity multiplied by the time in the air
4:03
so the range R equals u cos theta multiplied by the time of flight T
4:12
substituting the time of flight gives the range equation R equals u squared sin two theta over g
4:21
notice the range depends on sin two theta so angles that add up to ninety degrees give the same range
4:30
and the range is greatest when two theta is ninety degrees that is at forty five degrees
Time of flight
6:40
the time of flight comes from the vertical motion alone
6:46
the ball returns to launch height when its vertical displacement is zero
6:53
using s equals u t plus a half a t squared with s zero gives T equals two u sin theta over g
7:02
so a steeper launch stays in the air longer
Maximum height
8:15
at the top of the flight the vertical velocity is zero
8:21
using v squared equals u squared plus two a s the maximum height H equals u squared sin squared theta over two g
8:30
the maximum height depends on the vertical component only
Worked examples
9:40
first worked example a ball is kicked at twenty metres per second at thirty degrees
9:47
the range is twenty squared times sin sixty over nine point eight which is about thirty five metres
9:56
second worked example the same ball kicked at sixty degrees
10:03
sin one hundred and twenty equals sin sixty so the range is the same thirty five metres
10:11
but the time of flight is longer because sin sixty is larger than sin thirty
10:20
that is the end of the lecture on projectile motion
